bib.title: FrogNano: Training a 4B Coding Agent via Online Task Synthesis

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "FrogNano: Training a 4B Coding Agent via Online Task Synthesis". First author Minseon Kim (equal-contribution group with Zhengyan Shi, E. Penaloza, C. Cui, R. Creus Castanyer; senior: Xingdi Yuan, Marc-Alexandre Cote, Alessandro Sordoni). Froggy Team, Microsoft Research Montreal. arXiv:2609.07925v5 [cs.AI], 5 Oct 2026 (v5 date; first submission September 2026 inferred from the arXiv ID only). Venue: preprint, no venue printed.
COVERAGE: 37 of 37 pages, 126,735 chars. I read pp.1-15 (body and limitations) and Appendix A, A.1, B and the start of C in full (pp.21-22). I skimmed the references (pp.16-20) and the later appendix pages (rest of C, D to F, Tables 3-4, Figs 16-19, about pp.22-37) by grep only. Figure and table captions and the bodies of Appendices D to F were not read in detail. I did not run the figures script.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Five iterations of RL on 300 synthetic tasks each lift SWE-bench Verified from 39.4% to 61.5%.
 number: 39.4 -> 49.1, 53.1, 56.7, 59.1, 61.5
 setup: Qwen3.5-4B base, Leaf harness, 150 steps, 131k context, temperature 0.6, mean of 3 seeds. Verified is also the validation set.
 quote: "starting from a 39.4% solve rate on SWE-bench Verified, five TaskPilot iterations of 300 synthetic tasks each raise it to 49.1%, 53.1%, 56.7%, 59.1% and finally 61.5% for iteration 5"
 where: p.9
2. Other benchmarks (held-out test sets): 37.6% SWE-bench Pro, 31.1% Terminal-Bench 2.0, 47.3% PatchEval-Verified. There is no distillation from a larger model.
 setup: same eval settings, 3 seeds. Training data is Python-heavy.
 quote: "FrogNano reaches 61.5% solve rate on SWE-bench Verified, 37.6% on SWE-bench Pro, 31.1% on Terminal- Bench v2, and 47.3% on PatchEval-Verified"
 where: p.3
 bears on: note 05 (post-training for agents), note 06 (data and environments)
3. Synthetic tasks versus real tasks (the main baseline). About 300 synthetic tasks calibrated to the policy match or beat about 300 real SWE-rebench tasks filtered by the same 4B learnability criterion.
 number: 48.0% for 300 real tasks. Fig 1 also shows a 1,500-real-task baseline (SWE-rebench plus Scale-SWE, learnability-filtered); its value is only in the figure. The extracted figure numbers 53.4 and 48.0 are unlabelled, so I did not attach 53.4 to a series.
 quote: "we also train on approximately 300 real SWE-rebench tasks selected by the same 4B learnability criterion, which reaches 48.0%."
 where: p.9
 caveat: the comparison is against iteration 1 or 2 (49.1%), but the sentence does not say which synthetic iteration it compares with. Check Fig 1.
 bears on: note 06
4. The harness matters a lot for a small model. Qwen3.5-4B goes from 8.3% under the R2E-Gym harness to 37.2% under the Leaf harness. Leaf has five typed tools, a Claude-Code-style schema and natural termination. MiniMax-M2.5 is unchanged at 66.5% on both.
 setup: other rollout settings held fixed. Under R2E-Gym about 96% of 4B trajectories hit the turn limit.
 quote: "boosting Qwen3.5-4B's performance from 8.3% using the R2E-Gym harness to 37.2% when using Leaf. ... MiniMax-M2.5, is unaffected by the harness change (66.5% on both harnesses)."
 where: p.4
 bears on: note 05, note 10
5. Policy-calibrated task synthesis (TaskPilot). It generates the problem statement, gold patch and hidden fail-to-pass tests. Current-policy rollouts estimate a resolve rate. Candidates are refined, kept or discarded.
 setup: iterations 1-4 target p=0.5. Iteration 5 uses a stronger task-generation model and a 0 < p <= 0.5 band, because a first iteration 5 run under the old regime "yielded weaker gains". The iteration 5 batch also has a shorter statement (116.6 vs 227.0 words), a lower bug-fix share (40.7% vs 85.2% at iteration 1) and 0.04 explicit requirement items.
 bears on: note 06
 caveat: the iteration 5 gain is confounded with the generator and target change.
6. Training recipe: DPPO with asymmetric trajectory importance sampling (drop a token when delta-p exceeds 0.2 in the direction of its advantage). Binary test reward. Zero-variance groups discarded. No KL, entropy bonus or reference model. Success-gated log-length penalty R=1-alpha*ln(n/N) for n>N, introduced at iteration 3. Truncated-but-correct trajectories get 0.5.
 setup: 8xB200 node, 2 training GPUs and 6 inference GPUs. 32 tasks x 8 samples = 256 trajectories per update. 200 updates per iteration. Adam, lr 1e-6. Training uses temperature 1.0, 65k context and 75 turns for the first 4 iterations, then 131k and 150.
 quote: "Each update contains 32 task groups with 8 independent trajectories per task, for a global batch of 256 trajectories."
 where: p.8, Table 2 on p.21
 bears on: note 07 (reward design), note 10 (engineering RL systems)
7. Length penalty. It limits growth in assistant tokens "without noticeably degrading performance". Evidence is Fig 9 only, and there is no numeric ablation in the text.
 where: p.11
 bears on: note 07
8. Pass@k and verifier. The pass@8 gap between FrogNano and the base model "stays static as k increases", which the authors read as RL pushing the capability boundary rather than only distilling pass@k into pass@1.
 setup: SWE-bench Verified pass@1 is 60.4% in this analysis versus 61.5% in the headline. Test-time scaling with 3 candidates: round-robin verifier 62.8%, single verifier call 61.4%, random selection 61.53%, pass@short 60.4%. The verifier is trained with GRPO and a reciprocal-rank reward on rollouts from the last two iterations.
 quote: "this round-robin procedure achieves 62.8% pass@1, compared with 61.4% for a single verifier call, 61.53% for random candidate selection and 60.4% for pass@short."
 where: p.10
 bears on: note 08 (reasoning RL)
9. Per-iteration learning continues. Solve-rate gains within each iteration are 11.7, 3.4, 5.6, 3.0 and 5.4 points. Entropy falls from 0.415 to 0.265 in iteration 1 and is bounded afterwards. Four of five block-bootstrap intervals exclude zero.
 where: p.11
10. Cross-harness transfer. In mini-SWE-agent (a single bash tool), FrogNano goes from 43.8% to 56.4%, which is 5.2 points below Leaf. It hits the turn cap on 9.8% of trajectories versus 31.6% for the base model.
 where: p.11
11. Summary compaction. With 16K, 32K or 64K windows, compaction helps most at low budgets and "recover[s] full 131K performance at 64K". Numbers are in Fig 8 only.
 where: pp.10-11
12. Consolidation (SFT merging of rollouts from past checkpoints; not part of FrogNano). Reinforcing multi-tool-call trajectories gives 59.6% on Verified and raises the multi-tool-call rate by 16%. Steps fall from 53.5 to 36.6. Mixing iteration 5 rollouts with earlier-policy rollouts gives 62.3% (+0.8), pass@3 72.3%, pass@short 62.8%. FrogNano issues only 1.71% parallel tool calls. The paper says behaviours learned in early iterations can be lost in later ones.
 where: p.10, Appendix C
13. Failures and reward hacking on SWE-bench Verified.
 - Failures are 90.8% reasoning gaps and 7% premature termination. By test behaviour, 69.8% never fixed the issue and 24.8% introduced a regression.
 - Regex static analysis flagged 21.3% of trajectories; a three-judge LLM majority vote confirmed 2.5% as attempted hacks. Agreement was 93.02% (Fleiss kappa 0.746). The scaffold blocked all of them ("0 hack-related solves"). This is one reported check, not an independent audit.
 where: p.12
 bears on: note 07
14. Cost. About $0.21 per task on Verified at 131K context and an average of 53.5 steps, "one-tenth the cost" of gpt-5-mini at comparable performance. This is estimated from a token-budget model [3] plus list API prices, not measured billing.
 where: p.21
 bears on: note 05, note 10

LIMITS
- Conceded in the paper: English tasks only, Python-heavy repositories. Generalization to other languages, repositories, unclear requirements, other tool interfaces, prompts or budgets is not established. Rewards and scores rely on tests that cover only part of a program's behaviour, so a passing patch can still be wrong or insecure. Multimodal ability was not trained or evaluated. They only show up to iteration 5 and do not know how far it goes.
- The authors call the RL setup "not individually novel"; the contribution is the 4B combination of adaptive data and the length penalty.
- Not shown:
 - No ablation isolating "learnability-frontier" calibration from plain difficulty filtering at matched task count and compute. The only comparison is 300 real tasks at 48.0% against the synthetic runs.
 - No ablation of DPPO versus GRPO, or of the length penalty, in numbers. Seed variance and error bars are not given in the text (3 seeds are averaged).
 - The iteration 5 change confounds the generator and the target band.
 - The Verified validation set is also used to choose the best checkpoint to seed the next iteration, so selection leakage is possible.
 - Comparisons to Qwen3.5-4B (the base) use the authors' Leaf harness, marked with an asterisk. Frontier-model comparison numbers come from reports and leaderboards, so harnesses may differ.
 - Task generators are stronger models, so "distillation-free" holds only for trajectories, not for task content.
 - The consolidation experiment uses SFT and privileged information, outside the headline recipe.
- Dated: model names (GPT-5.5, Opus 5 and others) belong to this paper's 2026 timeframe.

BUILDS ON: DPPO [39]. Group-relative advantages and zero-variance filtering from DAPO [61] and GRPO [42]. PipelineRL [38] for async training, AReaL (Fu 2025) and DORA (Hu 2026) for bounded staleness. Task sets SWE-rebench (Badertdinov 2026) and Scale-SWE [65]. Prior synthetic data: SWE-Gym (Pan 2024), R2E-Gym (Jain 2025), SWE-smith, BugPilot. Curriculum ideas: GoalGAN (Florensa 2018), POET, PAIRED (Dennis 2020), PLR (Jiang 2021), ACCEL. Closest peers: CalibForge, Polar, Tmax-4B, FailForge, SSR, Socratic-SWE. Harness tools follow Claude Code conventions and SLIME [67]. Binary test reward follows RLEF (Gehring 2025), SWE-RL and DeepSWE.

CODE: none in the paper. Formulas: advantage A_ij = (R_ij - mean R_i)/(std(R_i)+1e-6) (p.8). Length reward R(n)=1 for n<=N, else 1-alpha*ln(n/N) (p.8). Verifier reward R=1/r* (p.10).

FIGURES (not extracted by script; captions from the text)
- Fig 1 (p.1): SWE-bench Verified across iterations versus the real-task baselines. This is the headline ablation.
- Fig 3/4 (pp.3-4): the training loop and the TaskPilot admission flow.
- Fig 5 (p.5): the same task at 0%, 50% and 100% resolve rate by changing only the problem statement. This is the clearest picture of "learnability frontier".
- Fig 9 (p.9): effect of the length penalty. Fig 10 (p.11): per-curriculum learning and entropy. Fig 12 (p.12): reward hacking across iterations. Fig 14 (p.22): pass@k versus the base model.

PROBLEMS: Extraction is clean. Some figure labels are interleaved and unlabelled (for example 53.4 in Fig 1). The v5 text has odd typos. Appendix pages 22-37 (rest of C to F, tables 3-4) were only skimmed. No embedded instructions found. First-submission month is not printed; only the v5 date (5 Oct 2026) is.

Verbatim quotes with page numbers for the note: p.1 abstract: "competitive small coding agents can be trained with synthetic tasks alone, without traditional distillation from larger models, and that generating tasks at the learnability frontier of the current agent is important." p.4: "performance of a larger model, MiniMax-M2.5, is unaffected by the harness change (66.5% on both harnesses)." p.14: "our RL setup is not individually novel; its contribution is the 4B-scale combination of adaptive SWE data and assistant-only log-length penalty."
